speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I make this Ministerial Statement to set out the framework of our policies; the reasons for our policies; and what more we intend to do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will set out the broader context for the situation – show how these criticisms are without merit.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will also set out what we intend to do about those attempts to abuse our legal process.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will cover four areas in this Statement.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, I will discuss the global and regional drug situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, I will speak about the threat from the drug trade and our approach to that threat.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And fourth, I will set out our plans to further strengthen our drug control policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every region, every region in the world is being affected by drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: European countries, first world countries, have been very hard hit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Europe's ports have been described by a major weekly as "drug hubs" and "safe terrain for narcotics".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also said that in the European Union (EU), half of all homicides and more than a quarter of illegal firearms seizures were linked to drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can consider just how many lives have been lost.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us look at some specific countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have set out on the slides, some of the quotes from senior people in the Netherlands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the port city of Rotterdam, children, some as young as 14 years old, are being recruited as "cocaine collectors" to get the drugs from shipping containers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The illegal drugs trade has grown "more lucrative, professional and ruthlessly violent".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Think of a Mayor of a major European city saying that and what the implications are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The chief of the largest police union in the Netherlands Jan Strujis has said the country had a parallel economy controlled by crime groups, shootings and killings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A former Justice and Security Minister Grapperhaus has said that "excessive violence" against politicians, lawyers and journalists was "no longer taboo".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sweden, considered one of the safest places in the world, has also been seriously affected by drug- and gang-related violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These were linked to fights between criminal gangs over drugs and arms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The then-police chief Thornberg said and, I quote, "citizens are afraid, insecurity is increasing".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Young lives in Sweden are being destroyed by this senseless violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2022, 30% of suspects for gang-related violence were between 15 and 20 years old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lawyer who represents teenage shooting victims and suspects told the BBC: children in Sweden are using their, and I quote, "own bags, not to carry books, but they carry the drug markets of Sweden on their shoulders." Turning to Belgium, last year, in Antwerp, an 11-year-old girl was killed in a shooting in her own home.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was linked to a drug-related gang dispute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the last decade, there have been hundreds of such incidents in Antwerp: shootings, grenade attacks, fires and bombings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many were linked to gang-related violence trying for a piece of the cocaine trade.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The mayor of Antwerp Bart De Wever has described the situation as being a "much bigger" threat than the 2016 Brussels bombings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Brussels bombings made headlines around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But with drug violence, it gets ignored even though it is much bigger and a more continuous threat which affects many more people and, really, this should be taken more seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their incinerators in Belgium were not able to burn the seized drugs quickly enough and the confiscated stash has earned the nickname "cocaine-berg".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Customs officials now tell the media that they will never win the war against the cartels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can ask themselves why are officials in a first-world country saying this: that they cannot win the fight against the narcotic gangs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), the example of Barrow-in-Furness shows how drugs can seriously damage a place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the last decade, the town has been plagued by drug use and drug-related deaths.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2018, its opiate-related deaths were double the national average.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It became known as the country’s "most infamous brown town".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, there was an almost 50% jump in drug offences compared to the previous year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The situation is dismal: town buildings mostly boarded up and vandalised, broken furniture strewn on the streets, windows smashed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Businesses and residents say that they may have no choice but to leave the town if things do not change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 2011 to 2021, the town population decreased by 2.4% while England's population increased by 6.6% over the same period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should have added in Belgium, the Justice Minister, my counterpart, has to live out of safe houses because the police cannot guarantee his safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us look at South America, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) said that 18 out of 21 countries are now the main sources of transit for cocaine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ecuador was once seen as a peaceful country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has become wrecked with drugs and violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 2018 to 2022, its homicide rates increased by four times and the homicide rates are now the eighth highest in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are reports of beheadings, car bombings, assassinations of police officers, children being gunned down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In one hideout used by the drug cartels, the police uncovered a collection of stuffed toys.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Gangs are said to have used the toys to attract young children and then recruited them as drug pushers and handed them weapons and forced them into the drug trade.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Mexico, murders, abductions, forced disappearances are almost daily occurrences due to turf wars between drug cartels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In recent years, some places have chosen to decriminalise drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They take the position that drug use is a personal choice and it should be destigmatised and allowed under certain conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Others say that the problem has gotten out of control and their solution is to allow drug abuse under so-called "safe" conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, they have decriminalised personal possession of drugs below certain limits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you know what police would do then?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They de-prioritised, decided that they will not deal strictly with open-drug use and small-scale possession.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A decade later, anyone visiting the city now will see people living in slum-like conditions along major streets, looking for their next fix.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some places, which chose to legalise drugs, have realised that the results were not as promised and have reversed their policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2020, the US State of Oregon decriminalised use and possession of small amounts of most drugs, including cocaine, meth and heroin.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fifty-eight percent of voters in Oregon supported it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police can then focus on other work and abusers would feel less stigmatised and abusers will seek treatment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But people in Oregon soon saw the results of this policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People felt unsafe on the streets, businesses started leaving and the situation got very bad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, the Canadian province of British Columbia decriminalised drugs to try and reduce its overdose rates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, the number of drug overdose deaths increased by more than 5% from the year before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was also public backlash against the open drug use.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Earlier this year, the provincial government tried to restrict the public places where people could consume drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Supreme Court blocked the measure, saying it could, and I quote, "cause irreparable harm" to drug users.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court said that users were at risk of overdosing alone, since they would have fewer public places to consume drugs and where people would be present.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Brad West, a mayor from a British Columbian city, said that the courts were out of touch with the public and blocking the measure, and I quote, "ignored the harm that occurs to others by allowing rampant public use".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last month, the BBC reported that the authorities in British Columbia were working urgently to re-criminalise the use of hard drugs in public places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My view to Members – when they experiment with laws like this, they are actually experimenting with the lives of people, including the lives of innocent young children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The policies and u-turns have a long-term impact on the next generation and the impact cannot be easily reversed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parents and guardians, if they become drug addicts, homeless and unemployed – it is the children who would suffer this proportionately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us look at a sobering personal account of a child who grew up in America with a mother who was a cocaine abuser: "From the ages of seven to 12, we were pretty much on our own.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, we would be left alone for days at a time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We would not have lights, water or heat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At night, we would huddle around the stove for warmth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It got so bad that we started hiding our mother's keys just to keep her from going to the crack house." In 2021, Gallup reported that about 32% of Americans say that drug use has been a cause of trouble in their family, one-third of all Americans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is almost double the proportion since 1999, when it was 17%.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Children and the next generation are the real victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A study estimated that in 2017, about 2.2 million children and adolescents in the US had a parent with an opioid use disorder or were affected by opioids themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The study projected that by 2030, this number would go up to 4.3 million – nearly double.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These children often do not have a proper home to grow up in, no role models to look up to and no stability to anchor their development.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without basic support, they have poorer educational outcomes, increased likelihood of developing substance use disorders and early emergence of chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, one has got to ask: who speaks for the human rights of these millions of children?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Closer to home, in Southeast Asia, the Golden Triangle, where the borders of Myanmar, Thailand and Laos meet, is a major drug producing region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The UNODC reported in 2022 that East and Southeast Asia are "literally swimming" in meth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2022 alone, 151 tonnes of meth were seized in the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the Committee of Supply, I spoke about the situation in Thailand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When cannabis was legalised, it was available immediately almost anywhere you looked – restaurants, convenience stores and even near schools.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within six months of legalisation, the number of addicts went up four times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were young teens and children who consumed cannabis-infused cookies, candies and sweets – they thought these were ordinary snacks – but ended up having to be hospitalised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Thai government recently has announced plans to reimpose a ban on recreational cannabis use by the end of this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One can see why but it is no longer going to be easy to do because if part of it is legal and part of it is not legal, then, enforcement is never going to be easy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In any event, businesses which have invested in the industry will likely push back strongly and those who are now addicted to the drug both will find it very difficult to kick off the habit and will need to be supported by the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The consequences, in many cases, can be irreversible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With that, let me now turn to the situation in Singapore and the threat we face here from the drug trade.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are a big target for drugs that this region is being flooded with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Despite our stiff penalties, some traffickers try their luck because of the profits they can earn.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The street price for drugs is much higher in Singapore than many other parts in this region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our purchasing power is much higher, our gross domestic product (GDP) is much higher, our wealth is much higher, so, it is obvious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) and Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) have found drugs at the borders in fire extinguishers, furniture, even fruits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People find many innovative ways of trying to smuggle in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the age of a Secondary 4 student.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can see that we are not exempt from the problems that other countries face.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We take an evidence-based approach towards drug control.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2019, we changed our policy to focus on helping persons who are pure drug abusers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they only abuse drugs and have not committed other offences, they are channelled to receive treatment and do not get a criminal record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The interventions are based on the risk profile of the abuser.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, low-risk, first-time adult drug abusers will generally undergo counselling in the community, together with regular urine or hair testing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This minimises disruption to their daily lives while ensuring that their addiction issues are addressed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond the mandated supervision period, the Singapore Prison Service (SPS) continues to work with Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG) and its community partners, to help the drug abusers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, YRSG assists ex-inmates with career coaching and job placement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many examples of ex-drug abusers who have kicked their habit, leading new lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He dropped out of secondary school, joined a street gang at the age of 12.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was involved in drugs and other crimes, including housebreaking and gambling, to feed his drug addiction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By the age of 32, he had already served close to 11 years behind bars, almost all his adult life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then, he decided to turn his back on drugs and crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is now 50 years old, married with four children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has stayed clean for more than 17 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should recognise not just the efforts of the ex-abusers to stay drug-free but also pay tribute to their families who support them in their journey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, we have invited several ex-abusers and their families to join us in the Public Gallery.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They show that it is possible to quit drugs and to live a fulfilling life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I ask Members to join me in recognising them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While we seek to help abusers, we take a tough approach against drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have zero tolerance for those who destroy the lives of others for money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The death penalty is imposed on persons who traffic specified amounts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The evidence shows clearly that the death penalty has been an effective deterrent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1990, we introduced the death penalty for trafficking more than 1.2 kilogrammes of opium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the four years that followed, there was a 66% reduction in the average net weight of opium trafficked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A 2021 study was conducted in parts of the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are evidence-based so I told my Ministry let us do a survey from the regions where many of our drug traffickers come from, to see what the population in those areas think about our penalties and are our penalties sufficient deterrent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because you deal with the drug situation by dealing with both supply and demand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Demand in Singapore – through public education, through control measures, through active campaigning, explaining the dangers of drugs; supply – by controlling the amount of drugs that come in and through the use of deterrents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The implications are when the drug barons go around trying to recruit people to come into Singapore, people will be very careful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many would say no and if they do get tempted, they might say, "Well, I will only traffic drugs below a certain threshold amount".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it makes it much more difficult to traffic substantial amounts into Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who suggest that the death penalty can be replaced by life imprisonment should look at these figures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The deterrent effects of the two penalties are very different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not easy for us – Members, policy-makers, Ministers – to decide to have capital punishment as part of the penalties in law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the evidence shows that it is necessary to protect our people, prevent the destruction of thousands of families and prevent the loss of thousands of lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we maintain the death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have to understand – this is nothing short of a war.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I say that we are fighting a war and using that analogy, because that is the scale in terms of victims and lost lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Others in this region have used the analogy of war and that has drawn different sorts of responses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But people know here in Singapore we go on the basis of apprehending the traffickers, dealing with the situations in accordance with laws passed by Parliament and we fight the drug war within that framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the life expectancy of male Americans has come down for two reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is more than twice the number of deaths caused by firearms in the same year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The World Drug Report estimates that in the same year, 31 million years of "healthy" life were lost due to disability and premature deaths as a result of drug use.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are lives of fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, sons and daughters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I use the analogy of war.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am talking about a war against those who profit off the drug trade at the expense of hundreds of thousands of innocent lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To put it in the context of fighting a war, let me refer to a point that Bertrand Russell made referencing the Second World War.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He pointed out in his 1943 essay titled, "The Future of Pacifism", that "if war is to be prevented, there must be a clearly expressed willingness to go to war for certain ends".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other words, if you want peace, you have to be prepared to fight for it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would argue the same applies to the war against drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this war, we will have to decide: do we want to go soft and risk ending up like the countries I have spoken about earlier?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we want to become a "narco-state", or an "infamous brown town", or a hotbed for drugs and violence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People may say: no one is asking you to go soft.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have said, there is a clear difference between the deterrence effects of the death penalty as opposed to other punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be more robberies, house breakings and so on, because drug abusers will need money to buy drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Evidence shows there will also be more sexual assaults, more homicides and definitely many more people will die in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we take a strict approach, and our strict approach has saved thousands of lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That number has now come down by almost half.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All things being equal, the number of drug abusers in Singapore should have gone up in the last 30 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The supply of drugs in the region has exploded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That figure of 6,000 should be two, three times more because more people should be consuming drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By that alone, I say we have saved the lives of thousands of potential abusers and we have saved the lives of their families from the consequences of one person in the family taking drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Consequences can be, as we see from other countries: homicide, violence, break-ups, poorer outcomes for children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a pretty sad situation in many places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the war that we are fighting in Singapore and if we do not fight it or if we lose it, then thousands in Singapore will suffer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, everyone who is asking us to go soft on drugs or remove the death penalty, is in fact advocating for a different Singapore – where there will be more people dying; there will be more children affected; there will be more unfavourable outcomes, particularly on people of lower incomes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now move on to deal with attempts by some to undermine our approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People can see what is happening around the world, which is why I took some time to explain country by country some of the countries – first-world; South America; the US; this region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Despite that, in recent years, there has been a small group of people who attempt to mislead the public with misinformation on drug traffickers and the death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They seek to evoke sympathy by presenting an image of an unfair criminal justice system stacked against drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They publish videos, pictures, stories from the traffickers' childhood, sharing interviews with family members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has got a brother; he has got a sister; he has a child; he had a childhood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And portraying the trafficker as a victim of unfortunate circumstances.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He did not have money and therefore, he trafficked in drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But they leave out the facts of the cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They leave out the accounting of the harms caused to the victims of the traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do not give any voice to the victims, the number of lives lost or wrecked by drugs; and the reason the traffickers were trafficking the drugs in the first place, which is to make money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The victims also have wives, sisters, children, parents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you face financial difficulties, if you need money, get a job.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not have to traffic in drugs to make money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Earlier, I recounted some stories of drug abuse overseas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have seen shocking stories in Singapore too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She became reliant on him for sustaining her addiction and did not come forward with the truth for months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The next slide shows photos of a crime scene, where a man who was under the influence of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), brutally stabbed his own mother and punched his grandmother to death.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Drug abuse is not victimless and all of these are caused by the drug traffickers, whom people glorify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The next slide shows a heartbreaking case where a life was taken even before the victim had any voice of her own.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She was assaulted to death by her own father, who was a meth abuser.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The man burnt the body and hid it in a pot to conceal his crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Several studies have shown that the harms of drugs are far-reaching into the next generation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their babies could be born with congenital defects, such as respiratory distress syndrome or smaller brain matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The newborns may also suffer from drug withdrawal, increased risk of disease and even infant death.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But these facts and images are usually missing from the speeches, posts of those who campaign against the death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, there are baseless allegations, one-sided claims and half-truths.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These baseless allegations are also made in relation to prisoners awaiting capital punishment – I will call them PACPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They cast doubt on the process, the legal process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They cast doubt on the convictions and the sentences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Five parties – Transformative Justice Collective, The Online Citizen Asia, Andrew Loh, Kirsten Han, M Ravi – continued to make false statements alleging that a PACP was denied an interpreter during the recording of his statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This, despite the Court's clear statement to the contrary – a blatant, false attack on the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of these activists have helped to file unmeritorious legal applications on behalf of convicted drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Applications are often filed at the last minute and those who help with these applications often hide behind the PACPs and their families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In one case, there were seven post-appeal applications, all dismissed by the Courts because they were all without merit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Seven, one after the other, no basis, after the substantive appeal was dismissed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the seventh post-appeal application, the correspondent's email address – kirstenhan@hey.com – was provided by a family member to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This obviously does not belong to the family, but to perhaps an anti-death penalty activist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court dismissed that application, said it was a blatant and ill-disguised application to disrupt the carrying out of the sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other words, a clear abuse of the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The person, with the email account by the name of Kirsten Han, if she was involved, was helping in the abuse of process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on what the Court said, you can see what the persons who were assisting in the applications were trying to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is not a drug trafficker, but his applications are somewhat illustrative of the point I am making.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He killed a father and son – brutal murders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think people remember them as the “Kovan double murder case” – a 67-year-old father and a 42-year-old son.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, one of the victims was even dragged almost one kilometre along Upper Serangoon Road.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was sentenced to capital punishment on 4 December 2015 by the High Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal in February 2017, seven years ago.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of them are still ongoing and I make no comment whatsoever about those which are currently before the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those that have been dealt with, have all been dismissed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Act will seek to safeguard the administration of justice and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It introduces new requirements to reduce potential delays to proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if the PACP had already had his or her sentence upheld by the Court of Appeal, then he or she will be required to apply for permission to make a PACC application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be a streamlined procedure under which only the Court of Appeal may hear PACC applications and grant a stay of execution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As part of the application, the person will be required to state the grounds of the application and the reasons for not filing the application earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But even before the law has come into force, a post-appeal application was filed by 36 PACPs in September last year to challenge the constitutionality of that law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal said the PACPs had no standing to bring such a challenge and the fact that such a challenge has been brought at all, spoke only to the PACPs' abuse of the process of the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just one day after the appeal was dismissed by the Courts, 36 PACPs, of whom 34 were the same parties involved in earlier post-appeal applications, filed another post-appeal application, relying now on some other matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I make no comment on the merits of those current applications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My comments about unmeritorious applications, abuse of process, all other similar comments, apply only to applications which have been determined by the Courts and dismissed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I rely on what the Courts themselves have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not the first time that large groups of PACPs have jointly filed applications to the Court, after all avenues of appeal and clemency have been exhausted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the past few years, there were at least five other such jointly filed applications, each involving more than 10 PACPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PACC Act, when it comes into force, will deal with many such applications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are now considering, what else needs to be done to make sure that this new legislation can be properly supported.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will come back to the House, if necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I wish to make it clear to Members and Singaporeans: be assured, we will take all necessary steps to ensure that this sort of abuse of process is dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now speak about the strong public support for our drug control approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is broad support from our population because we have been upfront and open about the rationale, circumstances and the safeguards on the use of the death penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Surveys conducted the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) show that support for the death penalty has, in fact, gone up in the last two years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a statistically significant increase of about three percentage points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The 2021 survey also found that about 66% of the respondents agreed or strongly agreed that the mandatory death penalty is an appropriate punishment for trafficking a significant amount of drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the 2023 survey, last year, 69%, almost seven in 10, agreed or strongly agreed, again, a statistically significant increase.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA will be publishing the full report later this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is quite remarkable because Members might sometimes come across activists and others saying: the death penalty is controversial, support for it is weakening and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, on the contrary, we are seeing the reverse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Support for the death penalty has, in fact, increased in a statistically significant way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It shows that Singaporeans understand the need for the death penalty to deal with the most serious crimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2023, the National Council Against Drug Abuse (NCADA) conducted a survey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And 87% agreed that our drug laws are effective in keeping us relatively drug-free.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have these high levels of support because Singaporeans trust the Government to do the right thing and to do right by Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My colleagues and I have engaged thousands of Singaporeans on this issue in just the past year alone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when Mr Richard Branson comes in to argue, he does not realise that we take our duties seriously, we are accountable to Singaporeans, we speak with thousands of them every year and we know what Singaporeans support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the vast majority of Singaporeans know and understand the facts and reality, and why the Government says the death penalty is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We formed the Inter-Ministry Committee (IMC) on Drug Prevention for Youths last year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke about this at the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members of the IMC have started running anti-drug programmes to enhance awareness on the harms of drugs and mobilise key community leaders and amplify our anti-drug messages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our schools will cover drug-related topics in their school curricula by extending it to other subjects, such as General Paper, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is for our communities to rally together to remind ourselves of the harm, hurt and trauma which the families and loved ones of drug abusers suffer and have suffered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our aim is to drive home the message that the harms drugs cause are far-reaching and require a strong response from society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In partnership with CNB, schools and IHLs will be organising various activities, such as lessons, exhibitions and talks on the Remembrance Day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will also be an essay competition for youths in post-secondary educational institutions to encourage conversations and reflections on the impact of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a major step that we are taking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By this, we hope to bring across to a larger segment of the population, particularly the young, in a very impactful way, or as an impactful way as possible, the harm that drugs cause.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But of course, it will include victims in Singapore, including the elderly mother and grandmother brutally murdered, the two-year-old toddler who was senselessly assaulted to death by her own guardian, and the countless family members whose lives have been upended by having a loved one going to drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are the people who deserve our sympathy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I strongly encourage Singaporeans to visit the exhibitions, participate in these activities, to be aware of the global and local drug situation and to show solidarity in our fight against drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the drug situation continues to be challenging, abroad certainly, but at home as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have to respond robustly to these challenges so that we do not have a generation caught up with drug addiction, so that our children can inherit a country that is safe and free of drugs and have the same environment that we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now have clarifications on the Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can seek clarifications by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Likewise, I would ask the Minister to also keep his answers clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, I understand the same report covered some information on preventive education and efforts taken at preventive education.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What other new initiatives can we expect with regard to the increasing number of abusers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Related to this, there has been a significant jump in new psychoactive substances which have been seized by CNB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there a particular reason why there has been an evolution from other drugs, which are classified in the report, to these new psychoactive substances being abused in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be helpful if the Minister could share with us whether this is across the board or are there specific communities that are consuming these new drugs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question refers to the slide that the Minister put up on the two-year recidivism rate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The final clarification is with regard to the recently passed Post-Appeal Applications in Capital Cases Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister suggested that we may come back to the House to see what else needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the Minister suggesting that there are some gaps in the Bill, which has not even come into force yet, which may require an amendment to the Act as it stands?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I look forward to support from Mr Singh if we were to come for that, since this is a fight that all of us have to take seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the answer is, we looked at what we needed to do and we passed the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have seen how the applications have evolved and I have directed my Ministry – I have not said there are any gaps – to look to see whether we need to do anything more, given in particular that there was a constitutional challenge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We disclose everything, we put the data out there and be transparent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a problem, and CNB and my Ministry said that there is this problem.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to do even better at preventive drug education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to focus on the parents as well to understand the messages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the other new initiatives, I have spoken about them in my Ministerial Statement earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question on psychoactive substances – why is there a jump?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, you can alter chemical properties and create drugs fairly easily and they become easily available.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every time you identify a compound, someone else can very quickly alter one or two chemical properties and come out with a technically different compound but with the same impact as the original compound.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is a continuous chase and you have to continuously deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And because now it can be produced in a lab, as it were, it is also much easier to produce larger quantities and some of it have properties that some of our young find attractive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to whether the five-year recidivism rate has come down over the 30-year period, I would ask the Member to file a Parliamentary Question and we will deal with it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I think one would also need to take note that, coupled with the tough stance, is a compassionate stance in helping the drug victims and the family.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And the presence of the families here in the House is a clear articulation of that approach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had regard to a research paper in 2022 where it was highlighted that in relation to so called "soft drugs", there were positive perceptions of these so called "soft drugs" in 75% of 16 million posts that were analysed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our young consume social media for news and they are exposed to this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The last point is the fact that increasingly – and this, perhaps, is my personal perception – Singapore seems to be, in a sense, set aside in relation to conferences dealing with the drugs issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I myself have had a chance to articulate Singapore's strong anti-drugs stance in a symposium in Cambridge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I was referred to as having outlier arguments and Singapore's experience cannot be replicated elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How do we make sure that our children from Gen Z and Gen Alpha would understand and internalise our strong anti-drugs policy?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at these international conferences, the NGOs which are taking a tough line on drugs are usually poorly financed, their material is not so attractive; whereas on the other side, there are all these glitzy arguments as to why soft drugs, cannabis cause you no harm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is just something for you to try, it is cool.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the whole idea of the "cool" factor pushed at our young from media, online, friends, peer pressure; wherever you turn, it is there and it is glamourised today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you ask why is there a jump amongst our young in, albeit from a lower base, the answer is obvious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is very difficult to stand against this multi-faceted assault.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think we have done a reasonably good job.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We usually get one of two reactions: one, a sullen silence as we put out our statistics and situation, because people just do not like it; the second is, "Well, you know, yes, we accept that Singapore succeeds but what you do cannot be replicated elsewhere".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it can be, but it is not for me to fight the fight in the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As long as others do not tell us what to do and leave us alone to protect our population, then I think that is the best that we can hope for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second Minister Josephine Teo goes very regularly to the UN conference on drugs in Vienna.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We put forward our position and, yes, we are somewhat isolated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are other countries which take a tough approach, but I think none put forward the arguments quite in the way that we do, presented with research and statistics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we do have a group of countries that take a view against drugs, including in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are differences of view, but never underestimate, it is a very tough environment to get our message across to our own people and we will all have to continue to fight on it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Preventive drug education is a broad title, but CNB and MHA is trying many different things now to try and get the message across even better, even clearly and to more people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think if you go and ask, those of you with primary school children; ask them, I think they would have heard about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will tell you what they have been told.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The next question is trying to get it to be imbued in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there, I am hoping that our initiative on Drug Victims Remembrance Day would help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other steps that we are taking, I am hoping will help.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When I was in primary school, there were campaigns against glue sniffing, which was seen as a gateway drug.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Are there any other gateway substances or drugs that the public should be aware of and which the youths in particular should be aware of today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some might, for example, refer to vaping as a gateway and for that, the Ministry of Health will answer as to what steps they are taking.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any more clarifications from Members for the Minister?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Order of the Day.
